evidence_quotes.quote: The plant is also operating well below its intended capacity because of delays in getting the town’s residents and businesses to connect to the system.

Initial rules set by the municipality actually discouraged property owners from connecting to the system because they demanded that users demonstrate legal ownership of the property and be up to date with other tax bills. These requirements were subsequently lightened: a user requesting sewage connection need only be current with payments for trash collection and water supply, then pay a connection fee of Q75 (about $9.40).

Of some 1400 households recorded by the municipal government, slightly more than half had been approved for connection by April 2001, and 550 connections were operating. Three of the 8 major hotels were connected and paying their fees, as were 6 of some 40 guesthouses.

drew on an existing body of prior interview data in reconstructing the historical context, and held discussions with key persons who had since departed the local scene, including the lead designer of the plant and the town’s former mayor who championed the project.
Under the new agreement, neighbors must form an alley committee in which all alley residents commit to connect to the sewage system.
In March 2002, three densely populated alleyways were working with the municipality under this type of agreement to connect 185 additional families to the system.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines household and commercial connection to a municipal wastewater collection and treatment system (sewerage service access) as well as historical transition to piped municipal water supply in Panajachel, Guatemala.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies Criterion 2 under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading. Under the plain reading, the study examines municipal governance, state administration versus traditional Mayan communal institutions, and stakeholder co-governance of wastewater infrastructure. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, the study directly analyzes concrete municipal eligibility, documentation/tenure, administrative burden, tariff/cost-recovery, and accommodation rules governing household sewer connections: (1) initial municipal connection rules requiring proof of legal property ownership and clearance of municipal tax arrears, which discouraged connections; (2) revised eligibility rules requiring applicants to be current on water supply and trash collection bills plus a Q75 connection fee; (3) user-fee/tariff cost-recovery structures and proposed progressive differential tariffs between households and tourism businesses; and (4) municipal collective alleyway agreements requiring neighborhood committee formation, collective payment clearance, and resident labor co-production in exchange for municipal piping and alley paving.
criterion_notes.c3: Empirical qualitative action-research case study conducted between January 2001 and September 2002, drawing on stakeholder interviews, historical interview data, a multi-stakeholder forum in April 2001, and municipal administrative and financial records on sewer connections, fees collected, and operating costs. Per protocol rules, qualitative socio-legal empirical studies are eligible for systematic review inclusion.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports concrete service access, connection, exclusion, and affordability outcomes: out of roughly 1,400 municipal households, slightly over half were approved for sewage connection and 550 connections were operating by April 2001 (plus 3 of 8 major hotels and 6 of about 40 guesthouses); exclusion/non-connection driven by legal-title requirements, tax/fee arrears rules, and unaffordable connection/user fees relative to low household incomes; and 185 additional families across three densely populated alleyways connecting under the March 2002 collective alley-committee rules.
criterion_notes.c5: Identifies population and units of analysis (municipality, neighborhoods/alleyways, and roughly 1,400 households plus hotels/guesthouses in Panajachel, Guatemala), exposure (municipal sewer connection documentation/tenure and tax/utility-arrears eligibility rules, connection/user tariffs, and collective alleyway co-production agreements), outcome (household and business sewer connections, fee compliance, and affordability/exclusion), and study design (qualitative action-research case study).

study_design: Qualitative action-research case study (interviews, stakeholder consultations, and municipal administrative data, January 2001-September 2002)
population_and_sample: Households (approximately 1,400 recorded by the municipality; 7,339 permanent residents in 1994 census), tourism businesses (8 major hotels and approximately 40 guesthouses), and municipal/NGO/community stakeholders in Panajachel, Lake Atitlán, Guatemala (units of analysis: municipality, neighborhood/alleyway, and household/property)
exposure: Municipal sewer connection eligibility and documentation rules (initial requirement to prove legal property ownership and municipal tax clearance; revised requirement to be current on water and trash bills plus a Q75 connection fee), tariff/user-fee cost-recovery schedules, and collective alleyway committee co-production agreements
outcome: Household and business connection to the municipal wastewater/sewage system (approvals and operating connections), fee compliance, and affordability/exclusion barriers
rationale: This empirical action-research case study in Panajachel, Guatemala meets all inclusion criteria (c1-c6). It examines household and commercial connection to a municipal sewage/wastewater system (c1) and directly analyzes rule-type legal and administrative mechanisms governing service access under both the plain and narrow 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 readings—specifically municipal rules requiring proof of legal property ownership and tax clearance to connect, revised utility-payment clearance and Q75 connection-fee rules, user-fee/tariff structures and household affordability burdens, and collective alleyway connection agreements (c2). It draws on primary interviews (2001-2002), stakeholder consultations, and municipal connection/financial data (c3), and reports concrete household and business sewer connection and exclusion outcomes (c4, c5) in English (c6).
